nodes.summary: Let $m$ be a list of $n$ Boolean marks and let $u$, $v$ be natural numbers; write $m_u$ for the entry of $m$ at position $u$ (counting from $0$), taken to be false when $u \ge n$. If $u < n$, $v < n$ and $m_u$ is true, set position $v$ of $m$ to true, and otherwise keep $m$; the result is the same as setting position $v$ of $m$ to true when $m_u$ is true and keeping $m$ otherwise.
nodes.title: Out-of-range arcs need no guard

nodes.summary: For $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and a list $E$ of pairs of natural numbers, there is an arc from $u$ to $v$ when the pair $(u, v)$ occurs in $E$, $u < n$ and $v < n$; listed pairs with an end at least $n$ give no arc.
nodes.title: Arcs of the PATH digraph

nodes.summary: Let $m$ be a list of Boolean marks and $j$ a natural number. Drop the first $j$ marks of $m$ and write the rest as bit symbols; reading the top symbol as a bit, with false when there is no top symbol, gives the entry of $m$ at position $j$ (counting from $0$), or false when $j$ is at least the length of $m$.
nodes.title: Reading the mark of vertex $j$

nodes.summary: Let $l_1$ and $l_2$ be lists of booleans of the same length such that every position holding $\mathrm{true}$ in $l_1$ also holds $\mathrm{true}$ in $l_2$. Then $l_1$ has at most as many $\mathrm{true}$ entries as $l_2$, and strictly fewer if $l_1 \ne l_2$.
nodes.title: Counting true entries of pointwise dominated boolean lists

nodes.summary: For natural numbers $s, t, n$ and a list $E$ of pairs of natural numbers, the PATH instance parser applied to the PATH instance encoding of $(s, t, n, E)$ succeeds and returns $(s, t, n, E)$.
nodes.title: Decoding inverts the PATH instance encoding

nodes.summary: For a bit string $x$, natural numbers $s, t, n$ and a list $E$ of pairs of natural numbers, the PATH instance parser applied to $x$ succeeds with result $(s, t, n, E)$ if and only if $x$ is the PATH instance encoding of $(s, t, n, E)$.
nodes.title: The PATH instance parser succeeds exactly on encodings

nodes.summary: Writing $1$ for true and $0$ for false, a bit string $x$ is parsed by reading a unary number $s$ (a run of ones ended by a zero), then a unary number $t$ from the rest, then a graph from what remains: a unary number $n$ followed by pairs $(u, v)$ of unary numbers until the input ends. The result is $(s, t, n, E)$, with $E$ the list of these pairs in order; there is no result unless the input ends right after $n$ or…
nodes.title: Decoding a PATH instance

nodes.summary: Let $n$ be a natural number, $es$ a list of arcs $(u, w)$ of natural numbers and $m$ a list of $n$ Boolean marks. Encode an arc $(u, w)$ by $u$ ones, a zero, $w$ ones and a zero, and $es$ by the concatenation of the codes of its arcs; let $\ell$ be the length of this code. Suppose the marking machine is at the edge-loop label, in any internal state, with stacks $S$ such that the input stack $X$ holds the code of…
nodes.title: The edge loop of a pass

nodes.summary: Let $s, t, n, s', t', n'$ be natural numbers and $E, E'$ lists of pairs of natural numbers. If the PATH instance encodings of $(s, t, n, E)$ and $(s', t', n', E')$ are equal, then $s = s'$, $t = t'$, $n = n'$ and $E = E'$.
nodes.title: The PATH instance encoding is injective

nodes.summary: Writing $1$ for true and $0$ for false, the instance with source $s$, target $t$ and the digraph given by $n$ and the edge list $E$ is encoded as $s$ ones, a zero, $t$ ones, a zero, then $n$ ones and a zero, followed, for each pair $(u, v)$ of $E$ in order, by $u$ ones, a zero, $v$ ones and a zero.
nodes.title: Encoding of a PATH instance

nodes.summary: Let $d$ be a stack of the marking machine, $ps$ a list of pairs of a stack and a symbol, $i$ a natural number, and $S$, $S'$ two contents of the stacks. Suppose every stack $q$ other than the input $X$ and $d$ holds in $S'$ the list it holds in $S$ with $i$ further copies of the symbol of the first entry for $q$ in $ps$ pushed on top (and unchanged if $ps$ has no entry for $q$). Then $S'$ agrees with $S$ on every…
nodes.title: The frame of a read

nodes.summary: For a list $A$ of stacks of the marking machine and two contents $S$, $S'$ of its stacks, $S'$ agrees with $S$ off $A$ when every stack not in $A$ holds the same list in $S'$ as in $S$.
nodes.title: Agreement off a set of stacks

nodes.summary: For every decidable proposition $p$, the optional mark that is a cleared mark (false) when $p$ holds and absent otherwise, read with default false, is false.
nodes.title: A cleared mark or nothing reads as cleared

nodes.summary: Let $m$ be a list of booleans and $v, w$ natural numbers, and read a position at or beyond the end of a list as $\mathrm{false}$. Set the entry of $m$ at position $w$ to $\mathrm{true}$, leaving $m$ unchanged if $w$ is not less than the length of $m$. Then position $v$ of the result holds $\mathrm{true}$ if and only if position $v$ of $m$ holds $\mathrm{true}$, or $v = w$ and $w$ is less than the length of $m$.
nodes.title: Setting an entry of a boolean list to true

nodes.summary: Let $n, s, v$ be natural numbers, and read a position at or beyond the end of a list as $\mathrm{false}$. Position $v$ of the initial marks for $n$ vertices and source $s$ holds $\mathrm{true}$ if and only if $v < n$ and $v = s$.
nodes.title: The initial marks mark exactly the source, if it is a vertex

nodes.summary: For $n, s \in \mathbb{N}$, the initial marks are the list of $n$ booleans whose entry at position $i < n$ is true exactly when $i = s$; all entries are false when $s \ge n$.
nodes.title: Initial marks

nodes.summary: The marking algorithm for PATH, as a function from bit strings to booleans, is computable in polynomial time by a Turing machine with respect to the canonical bitstring encodings of lists of booleans and of booleans.
nodes.title: The marking algorithm is polynomial-time

nodes.summary: Let $n$ and $v$ be natural numbers, $E$ a list of pairs of natural numbers and $m$ a list of booleans whose position $v$ holds $\mathrm{true}$ (positions at or beyond the end read as $\mathrm{false}$). Then for every natural number $k$, position $v$ still holds $\mathrm{true}$ after $k$ marking passes over $E$ for $n$ vertices, starting from $m$.
nodes.title: Marks survive repeated passes

nodes.summary: The PATH marking machine, run on an instance with source $s$, target $t$ and $n$ vertices, has eleven stacks: the input stack $X$, the output stack $O$, the stack $E$ of the edge bits (reversed between passes), the junk stack $J$, the counters $S$, $T$ and $N$ for $s$, $t$ and $n$ ($N$ counts the passes left), the counters $U$ and $V$ for the endpoints $u$ and $v$ of an arc, the mark stack $M$ (with the mark of…
nodes.title: Stacks of the PATH marking machine

nodes.summary: For an instance with source $s$, target $t$, $n$ vertices and arcs $(u, v)$, the labels of the PATH marking machine are $\mathsf{rdS}$, $\mathsf{rdT}$ and $\mathsf{rdN}$ (read $s$, $t$ and $n$); $\mathsf{val0}$, $\mathsf{valU}$ and $\mathsf{valV}$ (validate the edge list: at a pair, inside $u$, inside $v$); $\mathsf{goS}$ and $\mathsf{backS}$ (walk to $s$ and set its mark, then restore); $\mathsf{pass}$ (the pass…
nodes.title: Labels of the PATH marking machine

nodes.summary: Let $n$ be a natural number, $E$ a list of pairs of natural numbers and $m$ a list of booleans. For every natural number $k$, applying $k$ marking passes over $E$ for $n$ vertices to $m$ gives a list of the same length as $m$.
nodes.title: Repeated marking passes preserve the length

nodes.summary: Let $n$ be a natural number, $E$ a list of pairs of natural numbers and $m$ a list of booleans. A marking pass over $E$ for $n$ vertices, applied to $m$, gives a list of the same length as $m$.
nodes.title: A marking pass preserves the length

nodes.summary: For natural numbers $n, s$ and a list $E$ of pairs of natural numbers, the marks after $n$ marking passes over $E$ for $n$ vertices, starting from the initial marks for source $s$, form a list of length $n$.
nodes.title: The final marks have one entry per vertex

nodes.summary: Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$, let $E$ be a list of pairs of natural numbers and let $m$ be a list of booleans, where $m$ marks $w$ when $w < |m|$ and the $w$-th entry of $m$ (counting from $0$) is true. If $(u, v) \in E$ with $u < n$ and $v < n$, $v < |m|$ and $m$ marks $u$, then the result of the marking pass of $E$ with bound $n$ on $m$ marks $v$.
nodes.title: A pass marks the heads of arcs with marked tails

nodes.summary: For every $n \in \mathbb{N}$, every list $E$ of pairs of natural numbers and every list $m$ of booleans, let $m'$ be the result of the marking pass of $E$ with bound $n$ on $m$. Then $m' = m$, or $m'$ has strictly more entries equal to true than $m$.
nodes.title: A pass either changes nothing or adds a mark

nodes.summary: Let $n, v \in \mathbb{N}$, let $E$ be a list of pairs of natural numbers and let $m$ be a list of booleans. If $v < |m|$ and the $v$-th entry of $m$ (counting from $0$) is true, then the same holds for the result of the marking pass of $E$ with bound $n$ on $m$.
nodes.title: Marks persist through a pass

nodes.summary: Let $n, s \in \mathbb{N}$ with $s < n$ and let $E$ be a list of pairs of natural numbers. Let $r$ be the list obtained from the initial marks (only $s$ marked among $0, \dots, n - 1$) by $n$ marking passes of $E$ with bound $n$. Then one more marking pass of $E$ with bound $n$ leaves $r$ unchanged.
nodes.title: Repeated passes reach a fixpoint

nodes.summary: For all natural numbers $n$ and $k$ and every list $es$ of arcs of natural numbers, one pass of the marking algorithm with $n$ vertices over $es$ (Mark Pass) maps the list of $k$ cleared marks to itself.
nodes.title: A pass sets no mark when none is set

nodes.summary: Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$, let $P$ be a property of natural numbers and let $E$ be a list of pairs of natural numbers such that $P(u)$ implies $P(v)$ whenever $(u, v) \in E$, $u < n$ and $v < n$. If $m$ is a list of booleans such that $P(v)$ holds for every $v < |m|$ whose entry in $m$ is true, then $P(v)$ holds for every $v$ whose entry is true in the result of the marking pass of $E$ with bound $n$ on $m$.
nodes.title: Soundness of a pass

nodes.summary: Given $n \in \mathbb{N}$, an edge list $E$ and a list $m$ of booleans (the marks), the pass scans the pairs $(u, v)$ of $E$ in order and, whenever $u < n$, $v < n$ and position $u$ of the current marks is true, sets position $v$ to true. A position beyond the end of the list counts as false and setting it changes nothing. Marks set earlier in the pass are seen by later pairs.
nodes.title: One marking pass

nodes.summary: The unit symbol of the counters of the PATH marking machine is the clause-end symbol $\mathrm{cl}$ of the SAT verifier's symbol alphabet.
nodes.title: The counter unit of the PATH marking machine

nodes.summary: Let $n, k \in \mathbb{N}$, let $es$ be a list of pairs of natural numbers with edge bits $b$, and let $m$ be a list of $n$ marks. Start the marking machine at the label `pass`, with any flag, from stacks on which $N$ holds $k$ counter units, $X$, $P$, $U$ and $V$ are empty, $E$ holds the reverse of $b$ and $M$ holds $m$, both as bit symbols. Then within $k(5|b| + 3) + 1$ steps the machine reaches the label `goT`,…
nodes.title: The pass loop of the marking machine

nodes.summary: If a bit string $x$ parses as a PATH instance with source $s$, target $t$, $n$ vertices and edge list $es$, then the marking algorithm on $x$ returns the mark of $t$ in the reach marks of $s$ (the marks after $n$ marking passes over $es$, starting from the marks on $0, \dots, n - 1$ with only $s$ marked, and none if $s \ge n$), where a vertex $t \ge n$ counts as unmarked.
nodes.title: The marking algorithm reads the mark of the target

nodes.summary: On a bit string $x$, the check decodes $x$ as a PATH instance. If decoding fails it returns false; if it yields $(s, t, n, E)$ it returns true exactly when $s < n$, $t < n$ and position $t$ of the marks after $n$ marking passes from $s$ over $E$ is true.
nodes.title: The marking algorithm for PATH

nodes.summary: The component machine whose stack indices, stack alphabets, labels and program are those of the marking machine, with its eleven stacks listed once each, in the order: input, output, edge bits, junk, the counters for the source, the target and the number of vertices, the counters for the two ends of an arc, the marks and the parked marks.
nodes.title: The marking machine as a host component

nodes.summary: For every bit string $x$, the marking algorithm returns the same answer on $x$ as the decision problem PATH.
nodes.title: The marking algorithm decides PATH

nodes.summary: PATH ∈ P (Sipser, Theorem 7.14). The decision problem PATH belongs to the class P of decision problems decidable in polynomial time. Here PATH accepts a bit string exactly when it encodes natural numbers $s$, $t$, $n$ and a list $E$ of pairs of natural numbers such that $s < n$, $t < n$ and $t$ is reachable from $s$ in zero or more steps along the arcs of $E$ below $n$, the pairs $(u, v) \in E$ with $u < n$ and…
nodes.title: PATH ∈ P

nodes.summary: PATH is the decision problem that accepts a bit string $x$ exactly when $x$ is the encoding of some instance $(s, t, n, E)$ with $s < n$, $t < n$ and a sequence $s = v_0, v_1, \dots, v_k = t$ with $k \ge 0$ such that each $(v_i, v_{i+1})$ is an arc, that is, a pair listed in $E$ with both ends below $n$.
nodes.title: The PATH problem

nodes.summary: The multi-stack machine program whose input lies on the stack $X$ and whose answer is pushed on the Boolean stack $O$. To read a unary number off $X$ onto a stack $d$, it pops a bit off $X$ and pushes it on $d$, repeating while the bit is true and moving on after the first false bit; an empty $X$ jumps to `bad`. nodes.title: The marking machine for PATH

nodes.summary: Let $n, s, t \in \mathbb{N}$ with $s < n$ and $t < n$, and let $E$ be a list of pairs of natural numbers. Start from the marks on $0, \dots, n - 1$ in which only $s$ is marked and apply $n$ marking passes of $E$ with bound $n$. Then $t$ is marked if and only if $t$ is reachable from $s$ in zero or more steps along the arcs of $E$ below $n$, the pairs $(u, v) \in E$ with $u < n$ and $v < n$.
nodes.title: The final marks are exactly the reachable vertices

nodes.summary: For $n, s \in \mathbb{N}$ and an edge list $E$, the reach marks are obtained from the initial marks of $s$ among $0, \dots, n - 1$ by applying the marking pass over $E$ with bound $n$ exactly $n$ times.
nodes.title: Reach marks

Suppose the instruction of the marking machine at a label $\ell$ is the unary read off $X$ onto $d$ through $g$ that pushes $ps$ for each true bit, repeats at $\ell$ and continues at $\ell'$. Suppose the instruction of the marking machine at a label $\ell$ is the unary read off $X$ onto $d$ through $g$ that pushes $ps$ for each true bit, repeats at $\ell$ and continues at $\ell'$. If $X$ holds, as bit symbols, $k$ true bits, then a…
nodes.title: Reading a unary number

nodes.title: The unary read instruction

nodes.summary: Let $u \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $m$ be a list of marks. Start the marking machine at the label `go1`, with any flag, from stacks on which $U$ holds $u$ counter units, $M$ holds $m$ as bit symbols and $P$ is empty. Then within $2u + 2$ steps it reaches `go2` if the mark of vertex $u$ in $m$ is set and `drV` otherwise (a vertex past the end of $m$ counts as unmarked), with $U$ and $P$ empty, $M$ holding $m$ again, and…
nodes.title: Reading the mark of a vertex

nodes.summary: For every list $A$ of stacks of the marking machine and every assignment $S$ of contents to its stacks, $S$ agrees with itself off $A$.
nodes.title: Frames are reflexive

nodes.summary: Suppose the instruction of the marking machine at a label $\ell$ moves the bits on top of $P$ onto $M$ one at a time, repeating at $\ell$ and continuing at $\ell'$ once $P$ is empty or its top is not a bit. If $P$ holds the reverse of a bit list $p$ and $M$ holds a bit list $q$, both as bit symbols, then in exactly $|p| + 1$ steps the machine goes from $\ell$, with any flag, to $\ell'$, leaving $P$ empty, $M$…
nodes.title: Restoring the parked marks

nodes.summary: For every bit string $x$, the marking machine started at its start label, with any flag, with $x$ on the input stack $X$ as bit symbols and every other stack empty, reaches the label `done` within $8(|x| + 1)^4$ steps, with the output stack $O$ holding exactly one entry: the answer of the marking algorithm on $x$.
nodes.title: Running time and output of the marking machine

nodes.summary: For a list of booleans, the list obtained by setting its first entry: the empty list is left unchanged, and a list $b :: r$ with first entry $b$ and remaining entries $r$ becomes $\mathrm{true} :: r$.
nodes.title: Setting the first mark

nodes.summary: For all natural numbers $n$ and $s$, setting entry $s$ of the list of $n$ copies of false to true (which changes nothing when $s \ge n$) gives the initial marks of $n$ vertices from $s$: the list of length $n$ whose entry $i$ is true exactly when $i = s$.
nodes.title: Initial marks by setting one entry

nodes.summary: For a label $\ell$, the statement of the marking machine that pops the top cell of the mark stack $M$ and, if there was one, pushes the set mark (the bit true) onto $M$ in its place; in either case it then goes to $\ell$.

nodes.title: Walking to a vertex and setting its mark

nodes.summary: The marking machine for PATH starts at the label that reads the source vertex $s$, in unary, off the input.
nodes.title: Start label of the PATH marking machine

nodes.summary: Let $\ell$ be a label, $v$ an internal state and $S$ stacks whose mark stack $M$ holds the bits of a list $l$ of booleans. Executing the mark-setting step to $\ell$ from internal state $v$ and stacks $S$ ends at label $\ell$ with some internal state and the stacks $S$ with $M$ replaced by the bits of $l$ with its first entry set to true (the empty list stays empty); every other stack is unchanged.
nodes.title: Effect of the mark-setting step

nodes.summary: Let $c$ be a stack, $\mathit{self}$ a label, $\mathit{fin}$ a statement and $S$ stacks in which $c$ is empty. For every internal state $v$, executing from $v$ and $S$ the walk step counted by $c$ that loops at $\mathit{self}$ and finishes with $\mathit{fin}$ gives the same result as executing $\mathit{fin}$ from internal state false and the same stacks $S$.

nodes.summary: The statements of the multi-stack Turing machine (TM2) model whose stacks carry the stack alphabets $\Gamma$ of the marking machine, whose labels are the labels of the marking machine, and whose internal state is a boolean.
nodes.title: Statements of the PATH marking machine

nodes.summary: For every list $m$ of booleans and every natural number $j$, the first $j$ entries of $m$ followed by the remaining entries with their first entry set to true (the empty list stays empty) equal $m$ with entry $j$ set to true (which is $m$ itself when $j \ge |m|$).
nodes.title: Setting an entry by splitting the list

nodes.summary: Let $A$, $B$, $C$ be lists of stacks such that every stack in $A$ or in $B$ is in $C$. If stacks $S_2$ agree with $S_1$ on every stack outside $A$, and $S_3$ agree with $S_2$ on every stack outside $B$, then $S_3$ agree with $S_1$ on every stack outside $C$.
nodes.title: Frames compose

nodes.summary: The output stack $O$ of the PATH marking machine holds Booleans, and every other stack holds symbols of the SAT verifier's symbol alphabet.
nodes.title: Stack alphabets of the PATH marking machine

nodes.summary: Let $A$ be a list of stacks of the PATH marking machine, and let $S$ and $S'$ be stack contents such that $S'$ agrees with $S$ on every stack outside $A$. Then for every stack $k \in A$ and every list $l$ over the alphabet of $k$, the contents obtained from $S'$ by replacing stack $k$ with $l$ still agree with $S$ on every stack outside $A$.
nodes.title: Updating a framed stack preserves the frame

Then there are a Boolean $v'$ and stack contents $S'$ such that, in at most $2|w| + 1$ steps, the machine goes from the validation label (at a pair) with state $v$ and stacks $S$ to state $v'$ and stacks $S'$ at the label that walks to the source vertex if $w$ decodes as an edge list, and at the label…
nodes.title: Validation phase of the PATH marking machine

nodes.summary: Let $c$ be a stack other than the marks stack $M$ and the parked stack $P$, let $u$ be a symbol of the alphabet of $c$, and let $\ell$ be a label at which the program is the walk step counted by $c$ that returns to $\ell$ (with some final statement). Let $j$ be a natural number, $p$ and $q$ lists of bits, $v$ a Boolean, and $S$ stack contents in which $c$ holds exactly $j$ copies of $u$, $M$ holds $q$ as bit…
nodes.title: Walking along the marks of the PATH marking machine

nodes.summary: Given a counter stack $c$, a label $\ell$ and a final statement $f$, the walk step pops the top of $c$. If $c$ was nonempty, it goes to $\ell$ after moving the top mark of the marks stack $M$, if there is one, onto the parked stack $P$: the mark is popped, read as a bit (a symbol that is not a bit reads as false), and pushed on $P$ as that bit. If $c$ was empty, it runs $f$.

Theory of Computation

can_prove.label: ready to prove
can_prove.meaning: Statement is in Lean and nothing it needs is blocked, so the proof can start.

can_state.label: ready to state
can_state.meaning: Everything its statement uses is in Lean, so the statement can be written in Lean.

conditional.label: conditionally proved
conditional.meaning: Proof compiles, but rests on an open statement without a recorded Lean proof.

fully_proved.label: fully proved
fully_proved.meaning: Proved, and every prerequisite is fully proved too.

inventory_checked.label: inventory checked
inventory_checked.meaning: Module inventory checked in full; it records inspection, not a mathematical proof.

inventory_pending.label: inventory pending
inventory_pending.meaning: Module inventory not yet checked in full; it records inspection, not a mathematical proof.

not_ready.label: not ready
not_ready.meaning: Needs more blueprint work before it can be attempted.

proved.label: proved
proved.meaning: Proof compiles, but something it rests on is not finished.

stated.label: statement formalized
stated.meaning: Statement is in Lean; the proof is not.
